name: Vigilius of Rome
knownFor: Bishop of Rome from 537 to 555. Made pope in place of Silverius, he was held at Constantinople through the quarrel over the Three Chapters and the council of 553, condemning them in 548, defending them in his Constitutum of May 553, and condemning them again that December.
dates: Made pope in 537, when Belisarius removed Silverius (the continuation of the chronicle of Marcellinus Comes; Louis Duchesne, as Loomis reports, gives 20 March 537; Procopius of Caesarea gives no year). Taken from Rome in 544 or 545, by Louise Loomis's date. Died in Sicily on his way home; a record of the time that Loomis reports gives 7 June 555, and Henry Percival gives the end of 554 or the start of 555
place: Rome; Constantinople, where he was held after being taken from Rome; Sicily, where he died on his way home
role: Bishop of Rome; before that a Roman deacon and the pope's envoy at Constantinople

keyWorks.title: Constitutum on the Three Chapters
keyWorks.about: dated at Constantinople on 14 May 553, by Otto Guenther's reading, while the council sat without him. By the account Percival prints from Bossuet, it condemns certain propositions of Theodore of Mopsuestia but spares his person, does the same for Theodoret of Cyrrhus, holds that Chalcedon found the letter of Ibas of Edessa orthodox, and forbids any further dispute over the Three Chapters

keyWorks.title: Letter to Eutychius of Constantinople (the Decretal Letter)
keyWorks.about: dated 8 December, which Henry Percival reckons as 553; it condemns the Three Chapters and cancels whatever Vigilius or others had said in their defence, citing Augustine of Hippo, who corrected his own writings

keyWorks.title: Judicatum
keyWorks.about: issued in 548, by Loomis's account, condemning the Three Chapters while holding to the Council of Chalcedon, and later withdrawn; the text itself is not in the sources used here

traces: The council of 553 condemned the Three Chapters in spite of his Constitutum, and he then accepted its ruling. Percival says the council was opposed across the West, with Milan in schism until 571 and a schism in Istria that lasted until 700.
Loomis says the quarrel over the Three Chapters brought a new schism between East and West, "which lasted seventy years".
remembered: The Book of the Popes gives a mixed life of him. Romans call him a murderer and the crowd throws stones after his ship, but he refuses the empress and, at Constantinople, is dragged from an altar rather than yield. Loomis judges that last account partly legendary.

Liberatus of Carthage and Victor of Tunnuna, stern defenders of Chalcedon by Mommsen's account, tell how he won the see through the empress Theodora. Theodor Mommsen says both were embittered against him "iusto odio", with just hatred, and calls him perhaps the worst of the bad popes.

uncertain: The scene of his leaving Rome comes from the Book of the Popes, which Loomis finds full of mistakes and calls often partisan in this part; she says the scene is told nowhere else. Louis Duchesne, whom Loomis follows, argues its author wrote no earlier than the time of Pope Pelagius the Second, who began in 579.

How he became pope. Procopius of Caesarea says only that Belisarius appointed him after sending Silverius away. Liberatus says the empress Theodora had him promise in secret to set aside Chalcedon and that she offered him money; Victor of Tunnuna says she drew a secret written pledge from him. Liberatus and Victor are both hostile to him, by Mommsen's judgment.

The letter in which he tells Theodosius of Alexandria, Anthimus of Constantinople and Severus of Antioch that he shares their faith. Liberatus and Victor copy it. Loomis, citing Duchesne, holds it must be a forgery unless Vigilius was a shameless double-dealer; Mommsen leaves open whether it is his or forged, and says it was taken as genuine at the time.

The death of Silverius. Liberatus, as Loomis gives him, says Silverius was handed to Vigilius's guards and starved on the island of Palmaria. The Book of the Popes says Vigilius took him into his own charge, sent him into exile and fed him 'the bread of tribulation', and that he died a confessor. Loomis judges the guilt to rest partly on Antonina, the wife of Belisarius, and partly on Vigilius.
Whether the letter to Eutychius is genuine. Percival reports that Harduin held the Jesuit Garnerius had proved it a forgery, and says the learned have generally accepted it as genuine.
The year of his death: 7 June 555 in the record of the time Loomis reports, the end of 554 or the start of 555 in Percival.
